summary:
Western Visayas stands under the national framework of the Philippines, where same-sex relations and trans identity are not criminalised and no provision of national law punishes a person for being transgender. There is no administrative legal gender recognition: the Clerical Error Law (RA 9048) forecloses a birth-certificate sex change, the Supreme Court held in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan (2008) that gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery, and a court order remains the only route. The SOGIE Equality Bill has been filed and stalled in Congress for 25 years, and no national anti-discrimination statute covering sexual orientation and gender identity exists. Protections are sub-national or sectoral, and one province in this region, Iloilo, is among the eight Philippine provinces with SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinances; the national inventory does not specify which of the 32 covered cities and municipalities fall within the region.

No episode of the trans killings documented nationally in June 2025 occurred in Western Visayas: the murder of 18-year-old trans woman Kierra Apostol, the shooting of a trans woman journalist inside a clinic in General Santos, and the arrest of a foreign national in May 2025 on a charge of raping a trans woman at a Batangas resort all took place elsewhere in the archipelago.

Western Visayas' documented episode of institutional gender-expression policing is a university directive rather than a legal measure. In October 2022 Capiz State University enforced a hair-and-uniform directive that excluded students perceived as trans women from the institution. The directive was gendered and binary: students were held to men's haircut rules, and Khaz-JP Padilla, who later graduated from the university, described the effect of the haircut requirement on her confidence ('Why is it that whenever I cut my hair... it feels like I'm losing my self-confidence?'). Padilla transitioned once pandemic-era online classes removed her from the haircut rule's daily enforcement.

An advocacy campaign by a legal-NGO network followed the October 2022 directive and challenged it. The campaign's outcome was recorded at the university's 21st commencement exercises on 7 August 2025, when Khaz-JP Padilla became the first openly trans woman to graduate summa cum laude from Capiz State University and served as batch valedictorian of the social work class with the highest Latin honour. The milestone is attributed to the advocacy campaign that followed the exclusion directive.

As a signal for a visitor, the Capiz episode is indirect. A trans traveller in this conservative provincial region should not expect to encounter the university directive itself, and should not expect the university's current rule set to be verifiable from the sources here. What the episode establishes is that gender expression in the region can be policed by institutional authority, in a setting where the national SOGIE bill's inactivity means no legislative remedy is available for such conduct and where no evidence of an operative local complaint channel accompanies the directive.
tangentialFactors:
Detention rules that follow birth sex rather than legal gender or lived identity apply throughout the Philippines and would apply equally to a trans visitor detained anywhere in the region. Transgender women are held with male inmates; at Manila City Jail, arrivals to the male dormitory have their heads shaved, and survival is organised through inmate hierarchies and informal same-sex 'weddings' with male inmates rather than through policy. The Bureau of Jail Management and Penology's documented response at Davao City Jail has been administrative segregation, transferring LGBT detainees in batches to the City Jail Annex 'to prevent abuse' alongside persons with disabilities, the sick and senior citizens.

Schools are a further documented site of harm nationally: a 2017 Human Rights Watch investigation recorded bullying and discrimination against gender-diverse students across Philippine schools while noting that law offered few remedies at the time. The Capiz State University directive of October 2022 sits within that documented pattern rather than outside it.

Access to documents governs more than identity does. The Armed Forces of the Philippines have permitted openly gay and bisexual personnel since 2009 and transgender personnel since 2017, with the uniform policy following the legal gender shown on the birth certificate, and the Code of Professional Responsibility governing lawyers was updated in 2023 to bar discrimination against clients on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity. None of these rules extend to a private university's grooming standards.

The 2026 travel-risk assessment that rates Manila 'Generally Safe' for LGBTQ+ travellers at 69 of 100, with trans travellers scored lower at 62 in the 'Exercise Caution' band, is a national-capital figure. It is not a measurement of conditions in this region and should not be read as one.
localsOnly:
For students and residents in Capiz, the October 2022 Capiz State University hair-and-uniform directive was the operative measure excluding students perceived as trans women, and the advocacy campaign that followed was organised by a legal-NGO network documented in a December 2025 case study. Khaz-JP Padilla graduated on 7 August 2025 as batch valedictorian of the social work class with the highest Latin honour, summa cum laude, and is described as the university's first openly trans woman to do so; her account attributes her transition to the escape from the haircut rule that pandemic-era online classes provided.

Iloilo, within this region, is among the eight Philippine provinces with SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinances, giving residents there a local statutory complaint route that is absent in much of the country. The national inventory lists 32 cities and municipalities with such ordinances but does not identify which ones fall in this region, so coverage elsewhere in Western Visayas is not established here.

Because no national SOGIE statute exists and the bill has been in Congress for 25 years, residents' recourse against institutional directives of the kind applied at Capiz State University rests on sub-national ordinances where they exist and on organisational advocacy where they do not. The university's current haircut and uniform rules are not documented in the sources reviewed here.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the October 2022 Capiz State University directive was formally rescinded, amended or replaced after the advocacy campaign is unresolved. The sources document the directive, the campaign and the August 2025 valedictorian milestone; they do not state the institution's current grooming or uniform policy, and the milestone itself is not evidence of a rule change.

The coverage of Iloilo's SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinance, including whether the ordinance applies to private educational institutions and whether it has been invoked in practice, is not sourced here. Which of the 32 listed cities and municipalities with SOGIE ordinances lie within Western Visayas is likewise not stated in the national inventory.

Conditions at Capiz State University in October 2022 are documented for students. Whether comparable directives operate at other schools, colleges or workplaces in the region, and whether any enforcement action has followed, is unresolved and not sourced.

No source in this inventory addresses border screening, name or gender-marker consistency at Philippine ports of entry, or the handling of trans traveller documents in Western Visayas specifically. Entry and screening expectations must be inferred from the national framework rather than from regional evidence.
